notes.hook: The counter-intuitive concept of pointing a space telescope down into Earth grabs attention instantly.
notes.clarity: The explanation of using the Earth as a cosmic filter for neutrinos is easy to grasp.
notes.payoff: Detecting a blazar nearly four billion light-years away directly validates the bizarre premise.
notes.visuals: Diagrams and title cards are legible and clean, though heavily reliant on graphic cards.
notes.loop: The final beat connects smoothly back into the opening statement about building a downward telescope.

Beat 4: Completed in 2010, the array captures neutrinos travelling in straight lines across the cosmos.
Beat 5: Atmospheric cosmic rays swamp neutrino signals by roughly one million to one.
Beat 7: The detector tracks upward-traveling particles from neutrinos that passed entirely through Earth.

rounds.better_than_last: It delivers a much stronger conceptual paradox in its hook than episode 120.

notes.hook: The concept of an observatory looking straight down through our own planet instantly stops the scroll.
notes.clarity: Each beat cleanly explains one step of the engineering and physics without jargon overload.
notes.payoff: Explaining that Earth is used as a filter to block surface noise delivers a clever, satisfying resolution.
notes.visuals: The South Pole auroras and array schematics are crisp, though multiple repeated frames keep it from a top score.
notes.loop: Beat 9 connects conceptually back to the opening line, though the phrasing is slightly repetitive back-to-back.

rounds.better_than_last: It explains an unintuitive counter-concept—using the solid planet as an astronomical filter—with sharper logical clarity than ep120.
